glossary.sense: 華嚴三昧: the samādhi named after the Flower Adornment (Avataṃsaka) Sutra.
teacher: National Teacher Xianshou says the Flower Adornment Sutra calls it the Flower Adornment samādhi. What is Huayan? He explains: broadly cultivating the myriad practices — we broadly cultivate the myriad practices — according with principle and forming virtue. This virtue comes from principle. These are only words; it does not matter. And this principle and virtue pervade the Dharma realm. What does "pervading the Dharma realm" mean? Measureless and boundless; the Dharma realm is our mind.

What is "pervading"? Without end, beyond time and space: that is called pervading the Dharma realm. "Pervading" means without limit. That is what our own self-nature has, called mahā, rendered in Chinese as 摩訶, and 摩訶 means great. How great? Measurelessly great, great without any edge at all: that is called pervading the Dharma realm, and it is what every being has.

When you understand this, you can realize bodhi. What does realizing bodhi mean? It means you can become clear about the bodhi you always had. Realizing here is realizing without anything realized: realizing is knowing what you always had — you know it, you understand it; that is called realizing. Realizing does not mean that I practise something in order to realize it. No: it is yours already, but you have found it,

you have come to know it; that is called realizing. It is not fetched from outside: what I always had, I have understood; that is called realizing. What do I understand? I understand that my mind pervades the Dharma realm, without any boundary. That is called Huayan. Now we know what Huayan speaks of: it speaks of the Dharma realm, of our mind.

glossary.sense: 九世 the nine times: past, present and future, each with its own past, present and future.
teacher: Now he draws the conclusion about our mind, and the conclusion bears on the whole of the Pure Land teaching. Listen: he says our mind has "nothing lost of large or small", and "a thought embraces the nine times". The nine times are ten thousand ages: nine stands for them all. "Long and short at once": all at once, in the present moment. What does he mean?

"Nothing lost of large or small" speaks of space: large and small is space. "A thought embraces the nine times" speaks of time. Large and small is space, measured as space; the nine times, before and after, is time. What does he say the mind is? "Nothing lost of large or small" means beyond large and small, beyond space: the mind goes beyond space. "A thought embraces the nine times" means it goes beyond time. Now you know what he is going to say.

So our mind can go beyond space and time. Why? Because our mind pervades the Dharma realm: it goes beyond space, and our mind also goes beyond time. Going beyond space and beyond time is explained in Chinese as measureless light, measureless life: life is time, light is space. Measureless light, measureless life: the four characters that are always close to us.

glossary.sense: 止 śamatha, cessation or stilling. 觀 vipaśyanā, contemplation or insight. The subjects of the fifth and sixth gates.
teacher: What is contemplation? Seeing through, seeing clear through, understanding completely the true nature of the universe: that is contemplation, as in Guanzizai — contemplation is clear understanding. What is cessation? Once you understand clearly, you let go. That is what cessation and contemplation mean: one is letting go, one is seeing through. We often hear people say "see through it, let it go". They are two, and yet one. If there is an order between them, you must first see through before you can let go: if you cannot see through, you cannot let go.

glossary.sense: 隨流 going with the current of birth and death; 返流 turning back against it, toward the source.
teacher: Good, that is the first section. Next: this essence of the self-nature, pure, perfect and bright, "following the current and taking on defilement, is not soiled". Here National Teacher Xianshou is stressing it once more: however much defilement there is, it is not soiled.

"Turning back against the current and removing defilement": however much defilement you remove, it does not become pure. How is this to be explained? It is only said once more. The mirror is like our mind: whatever is put before it, dirty or not, it does not change. And "in the body of a sage it does not increase": in the Buddha's mind nothing is added; in an ordinary person's mind it does not decrease. So the Heart Sutra says: all dharmas are marked by emptiness, neither arising nor ceasing, neither soiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing.

glossary.sense: 性起 nature-arising (nature-origination): the Huayan teaching that all things arise as the function of the one nature.
teacher: "Relying on the essence, function arises": the essence is nature; the function is the flourishing; this is called nature-arising. "Arising in response in ten thousand differences": what are the ten thousand differences? What the mirror shows differs in a thousand, ten thousand ways: that is the ten thousand differences, so it is called flourishing. In a word, how does the flourishing come about? From nature-arising. So the flourishing does not leave nature-arising, and nature-arising does not leave the flourishing.

The nature in nature-arising is emptiness: nature is emptiness, and emptiness gives rise to form. So emptiness and existence are not two; emptiness and form are not different; emptiness is form, form is emptiness. Why can emptiness give rise to form? The scripture says: "From non-abiding…" "Always so, past and present": what does "always so" mean?

Never having changed: so now, so tomorrow, so forever. That is called "just as it is". This phrase is easy to remember. It means: nature can give rise to the flourishing; and how does that come about? Just as it is: the cessation that is "just as it is". Can you understand? It is not about memorising the words of a Chinese lesson; memorising is no use — that is for exams.

He puts down the imputed nature, and there is practice. He puts down the imputed nature, so there is an imputed nature for him to put down: there is still something for him to put down.
